PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   THE OFFICIAL DESIGNATION OF NOVA SCOTIA ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-217, an Act respecting the official designation of "Nova Scotia", be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as some Members may be aware, this is one of my pet personal projects. It has a great deal of significance. It is a simple Bill: one page, one paragraph really. As I made clear at the start, the Bill is for the proper use of
proper nouns. It is as simple as that. It is not anti-anything. It is not anti-English or anti-French. It is not negative English or negative French. The fact of the matter is that my province is known as Nova Scotia. It was given by a grant of King James the First in 1621. I do not know, perhaps in those days a lot of people did not speak English or French. To avoid confusing people, they chose Latin. Nova Scotia is a Latin name. Translated to the English you get New Scotland. From New Scotland you get Nouvelle-Ecosse.
I have been trying in a quiet way since I became a Member of this House to have the official designation be that of Nova Scotia in federal documents. I am not asking to repeal or change all documents. However, since this Parliament has been looking very much to the future in many ways, be it the Meech Lake Accord or free trade, we should recognize the reality of proper nouns in the proper place. That is, Nova Scotia is Nova Scotia. It is not Nouvelle-Ecosse and it is not New Scotland. That is the whole purpose of this Bill.
I may come at this in another way in another session. If we are not going to have the proper use of proper nouns, then I am going to bring in a Bill to make sure that every name is bilingualized. Then we can really corrupt the language, be it English or French. If you are going to accept some of the reasoning I have heard in the past from people who have spoken against this Bill, that you have to be bilingual, then we should do that. I am all for bilingualism. I have voted for every bilingual Bill in this House-
[ Translation]
-and supported French wholeheartedly, and I wanted to speak French today.

The next time I bring in this Bill I hope to speak all in French. I want to try to get rid of the canard-and I will come back to that word-that this is anti-anything. It is for something. It is for the proper use of proper nouns.
My name is John Patrick Nowlan. That is J-O-H-N, not Jean. The name of my good friend, the Hon. Member for London East (Mr. Jepson), is James Jepson; it is not Jean Jepson. Wolfville is my home town; it is not Ville de Loup. Grand Pre is the ancestral home of Longfellow's romantic Evangeline. That is three miles from my home town. We are proud to call it Grand Pre. We do not call it Grand Meadow. My mother was born on Canard Street. We do not call it Duck Street. You know this better than I, Mr. Speaker, because your fluency in both languages makes me pale by comparison. I commend you for it. However, you have a heritage that perhaps I was not exposed to.
We have a man in the front benches, the Hon. Marcel Masse. If we are going to be bilingual, then let us make it Marcel Sledgehammer in English. That is the way it is. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) comes from a historic place on the North Shore called Baie Comeau. I do not think he
November 26, 1987

wants to see a Bill go through this House which says that Baie Comeau should be Comeau Bay.
In essence, what I have been trying to do here in my own small way is to have my province designated as Nova Scotia, period. Nova Scotia has a rhythm to it, a romanticism. Tourism is a big thing in Atlantic Canada and there is a certain romanticism to Nova Scotia.
This Bill does not penalize anyone who wants to use Nouvelle-Ecosse. There are a lot of Acadians from my province and people from la belle province who feel more comfortable using Nouvelle-Ecosse. Let them use it. This does not penalize anyone. It is for the proper use of proper nouns. Nova Scotia is Nova Scotia.
I mentioned my good friend the Prime Minister because he and I share many things. Many years ago I worked on the railroad. At that time, long before the Prime Minister had an interest in the Iron Ore Company of Canada, I was part of the survey crew that laid the centre line for the railway which went from a place called Seven Islands up to Schefferville, a brand-new town. During my lifetime, quite properly, Seven Islands became Sept-iles. The reason I got on to this issue of Nova Scotia was that the then Member for Trois-Rivieres would rise on a point of order every time Three Rivers was mentioned. He would hold up the charter of Trois-Rivieres.

His name is Mr. Mongrain, I believe. Yes, I am thinking about Mr. Mongrain, the Member for Trois-Rivieres.

Every time an Anglophone mentioned Three Rivers when he was in the House, he would stand and make his point. I got a ticket in Three Rivers many years ago and I was called to the police station. It was called Three Rivers then. Now it is Trois-Rivieres. I say that Trois-Rivieres is the proper noun in the proper place. Sept-iles is the proper noun in the proper place. The same thing is true for Nova Scotia.
We have some other beautiful provinces in this land of ours. We do not translate the name Ontario. That is the Iroquois word for "beautiful lake". We do not call it le bel lac or whatever. Quebec is Algonquin for "where the river narrows". Manitoba is Cree for "the spirit of Manitou". Saskatchewan is also Cree for "rapid current". We accept them for what they are, proper nouns in the proper place. We do not try to translate them, and I am trying to focus attention on the fact that I am not trying to be anti, I am trying to be positive with respect to the proper use of proper nouns. I want to maintain the romanticism of Nova Scotia forever. I do not want it diluted by translation.
The Americans coming up here are sometimes confused about a place called Nouvelle-Ecosse when we have been advertising Nova Scotia. That is a practical problem, but it is deeper than that.
Nova Scotia
What about the capital? How many Members appreciate the fact that Ottawa is Algonquin meaning "to trade or barter". A very proper name in view of the fact that the House of Commons is here, and I guess we trade and barter.
I am asking Members not to talk this Bill out this time. I am, I guess, trading and bartering to get this Bill to committee where Hon. Members will come to understand that nothing horrific will occur if we use the proper noun in the proper place. It is as simple as that.
There is a Member on our front benches who used to be a Minister, Roch La Salle. If we want to translate and bilingual-ize everything, why do not we call good old Roch "Roch the Room"? We could call my good friend, the Minister of Agriculture, John Wise, "Jean Lesage". Let us be consistent.
I am going to continue to bring this before the House as long as I am here. If I cannot get this done one way, I will bring forward a Bill which will put Members on the spot to ensure that every name is bilingualized.
One of our great Speakers was Jeanne Sauve. I had some problems with her from time to time. I did not think she was a great Speaker, but she is a very fine Governor General. Sauve is a perfect name for a Speaker. Let's bilingualize it and call her "Jean Saved".
The name Nova Scotia was given to us by the Charter of King James I in 1621. It is in the original BNA Act. We in this Parliament, with some division, have just passed the Meech Lake Accord which brought Canadians together and brought Quebec into the Constitution. It recognizes the distinct society which Quebec is. I understand that. I have some problems with the promotion of it as a province, but I have no problem at all with the preserving and protection of a distinct society. However, what is good for Quebec as a whole in terms of a distinct society is good for Nova Scotia in terms of its name. The name Nova Scotia is distinct.
I ask Members not to talk this Bill out but to refer it to committee. I am not asking that we go to expense or that we roll back all the legislation and regulations. However, I am asking that we recognize the use of proper nouns in their proper place.
I believe I have illustrated the fact that we will have some very oddball situations if we bilingualize every proper noun. A word is a proper noun because it is a name, and it should not be bilingualized. The names of some of the provinces can be translated from English to French, from British Columbia to Colombie Britannique, from Newfoundland to Terre Neuve, or from Prince Edward Island to Isle du Prince Edouard. I frankly think it is wrong to translate those proper names, but I do not argue that case. However, Nova Scotia is neither English nor French. It is Latin, and Latin it should stay because that is the proper use of a proper noun.

November 26, 1987
Nova Scotia

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   THE OFFICIAL DESIGNATION OF NOVA SCOTIA ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the words of the Hon. Member. Coming from Nova Scotia myself I take great interest in Bill C-217. I understand the Hon. Member's point of view. To most Nova Scotians Nova Scotia is, of course, Nova Scotia. Nova Scotia has a very proud tradition, as the Member said, dating back to the Charter which was granted many years ago. He mentioned the changes of names which have taken place in Canada, Seven Islands to Sept-Isles and Three Rivers to Trois Rivieres.
We have done the same thing in Nova Scotia. In fact, the oldest permanent settlement in North America was founded in the Annapolis Valley in 1604, four years before the founding of Quebec in 1608 by Champlain. In fact, Champlain was one of the founding group of the settlement which was initially called Port Royal on the Annapolis Basin. They experienced very difficult winters there and established an organization which is still known as the Order of Good Cheer. We have, however, changed the name from Port Royal to Port Royal.
One of the most important French forts and strategic points in Canada was at what is now Louisbourg. Louisbourg was founded by the French to guard against British attacks by both Britain itself and New England forces in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and to guard the entrance of the St. Lawrence River. It was founded in 1713 and captured in 1745 by New England forces and again in 1758 by a British army under the command of General Wolfe. Of course, Louisbourg was not originally called Louisburg but Louisbourg after King Louis of France. We changed that name after it was taken by the English in 1758. It certainly was not called Louisbourg anymore, but Louisburg.
We in Nova Scotia have made our own changes. That situation does not exist only in Quebec. We have French translations for a lot of the provinces in Canada, Nouveau Brunswick for New Brunswick and Colombie Britannique for British Columbia. Therefore, Nova Scotia is not unique in that regard except that Nova Scotia is not English but Latin. There is a distinction in that regard. That is not to say, however, that the French language cannot translate Latin as well as it can translate English. Nova Scotia in Latin, of course, means New Scotland and the French translation is very accurate. Therefore, the French language has not really changed the meaning, only the language and I think it has respected the name.
This country takes pride in having two founding peoples and two languages, and I think it is of paramount importance that all Canadians respect the bilingualism of this country. I believe that to say that we will not allow French-speaking Canadians to call Nova Scotia by the name they have called it for many years is an infringement on their rights considering that they have accurately translated the name since Nova Scotia was founded by the French in 1604.
Perhaps the Hon. Member can tell me exactly what the feelings of the Acadians in Nova Scotia are with regard to this particular Bill because I think that is very significant. If they
wanted Nova Scotia referred to as is requested in this Bill, Nova Scotia, that would have a great deal of impact on my thinking. I have not done the research which the Hon. Member has done so I do not know what the Acadians want. However, until I know their thinking on this issue I think that to change it may be a presumption on their wishes, which I would not want to make at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on this Bill put forth by the Hon. Member. I find it somewhat strange that the Hon. Member has put so much effort into trying to tell French-speaking people what words to use and how to speak their own language.
The Hon. Member has brought similar Bills before the House of Commons on previous occasions. Apparently he had no support from the francophone Members of the House and, indeed, the Member who just spoke was very interested in knowing what Acadians thought of this Bill. I am pleased to be able to tell him.
The organization of Acadians, known as La Federation Acadienne de la Nouvelle Ecosse say that the choice of what to call Nova Scotia is theirs. Francophones have called Nova Scotia by the name la Nouvelle Ecosse for as long as it was known as Nova Scotia by Anglophones.
I do not believe this House should tell people how to speak their own language. It would be very different if this were a long-standing error that the Government had made.
The Hon. Member suggests that since the name Nova Scotia is Latin, it ought not to be translated. I suggest to him that many words in the English language have their roots in Latin. When I consider this Bill, I wonder if it is the terra incognita of the Hon. Member's mind that makes him make such an effort to bring this Bill before the House.
The real problem facing francophones in Nova Scotia does not include the designation of the name of the province, rather, it is getting proper services in French.
The organization FANE and Acadians in Nova Scotia generally, as well as my Party in that province, have made great efforts to obtain services and an official languages policy in that province. While such a designation has apparently been achieved, it is somewhat less than desirable.
I am surprised that the Hon. Member would persist with this type of legislation rather than fight for the rights of Acadians and francophones in general in Nova Scotia. There are approximately 30,000 people in Nova Scotia who have French as their mother tongue, and approximately another 8,000 with French and English as their mother tongue. This represents 4.5 per cent of the population of Nova Scotia, which is a significant portion of the province which has been fighting for improved services and recognition by the provincial
November 26, 1987

Government. That group refers to Nova Scotia as la Nouvelle Ecosse.
The Hon. Member states that the BNA Act was written in English, for which there was never an official French translation. That does not matter. We must respect the rights of people who speak any language to choose how they will refer to a province, a river, a company or a country. There are French names for Great Britain, England, Germany and many other countries that are different from the names used by the people of those countries. I suggest it would be very highhanded for this House to consider passing a Bill that would require French speaking people in this House, in referring to Nova Scotia, to use words which are of the Member's choosing and not theirs.
I do not believe there is any reason why the House should pass a Bill that would force Members to refer to an area in a language that is not of their own choosing.
There are many places in my own province that are referred to in English, Basque, Portuguese and French. These places were given those names by the people who travelled to Newfoundland, fished in Newfoundland and worked there. These places are referred to in English and in French.
My province is known as Terre Neuve by the Frenchspeaking people.
This Bill is a waste of time for the House. It is trivial, frivolous and pedantic. It ought not to receive the support of the House.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   THE OFFICIAL DESIGNATION OF NOVA SCOTIA ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments about Bill C-217 on the official name of Nova Scotia, which is sponsored by the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan).
The Hon. Member, who is a good friend, told us earlier how certain phrases can be translated from French to English, but I am convinced that he forgot a very important one. Mr. Speaker, I am not taking this example because he sits with the Opposition, but if we were to translate the name of the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) into English, we could end up with something like "bad pig". Unfortunately, there are certain things which can be translated and others which cannot.
Then, there is our friend, the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais), whose name could be translated as "A day was just born". Naturally, we can all play these little word games, Mr. Speaker, but the fact is that, as everyone knows, this Bill has been before the House four times without being approved. I believe that this fact by itself is an indication, and I shall come back to it. Since it has already been before the House three times, the Members who were there had the opportunity to hear many arguments for or against the Bill,
Nova Scotia
and those who were not always have the possibility of reading Hansard.
As we know, this Bill is quite simple. Its purpose is to ensure that the official designation of Nova Scotia remains "Nova Scotia" in legal acts in both French and English. The reason given by the sponsor is quite logical. When King James I gave that land to Sir William Alexander in 1621, the act of transfer designated the land under the Latin name of "Nova Scotia". The Hon. Member pointed out that, while official bilingualism leads us to translate certain geographic names from French to English and vice versa, we have no reason to do so for Latin names, no more than for the many native words which are so characteristic of the geographic designations in this country.
In terms of linguistics, since this is really what concerns us here, I would first like to mention that when the term "Nou-velle-Ecosse" is used in French, it is not meant to be a Translation of the term "Nova Scotia". Rather, I would say that it is the manner in which the French language refers to the same reality, just as it does in the case of many other realities, geographic or other. For example, when one uses the term "Germany", also of Latin origin, in English, or the term "Allemagne", which is also derived from Latin, in French with the same meaning, one does not usually stop to think that the Germans themselves call their country Deutschland. Obviously, the same can be said of a great number of other countries and regions of the world. What would be at the root of such a strange phenomenon? I cannot really say and in fact I would rather leave that to linguists and etymologists. However, I believe that even a layman can draw a few useful conclusions in terms of this debate.
The example I have just given shows that if geographic names can be so different from one language to the next it would seem to be mainly for historical reasons, given the fact that the terms "Allemagne", "Germany" and "Deutschland" have absolutely nothing in common except that they refer to the same reality. It seems also that the strength of usage and tradition as well as a certain emotional dimension, which may of course vary from one culture to another, also play a major role. I would even go further and add that the various designations which have stood the test of time are often the mark of the historical fame which those territories have gained. It could be said that cultures acknoweledge one another in this way. Even if we are dealing here with proper nouns, these terms have become part and parcel of a language.
It may also be noted that this is often explained for strictly phonetic or graphical reasons. To use a striking example, the great country that we call in French "Espagne" and in English "Spain" is being called "Espana" by its own citizens. The same thing for "Italie", "Italy" and "Italia".
Coming back home, I was suggesting earlier that "Nouvelle-Ecosse" was the French way of designating the beautiful province of the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants. Secondly, the terms "Nova Scotia", although originally latin, certainly are no longer perceived as such, so much so that latin

November 26, 1987
Nova Scotia
is a "dead language", but rather as the English name of the same province. Would it be that such a difference between the two languages stem from historical and emotional reasons, or simply from phonetic reasons as I just explained? I am not quite sure about that. But I have a feeling that it is both, which is healthy in a country that is committed to bilingualism.
Official bilingualism indeed is one of this country's basic values and features, and in order to be practical, it implies that all Canadian men and women, with the highest respect for the cultural nature of our two official languages, can make compromises that at times may appear acrobatic if we are to survive as a bilingual nation.
Therefore, I would urge all Members in this House to think about all the implications of this measure if it were enacted. I remind them also, as I said at the beginning, that this House has already considered this Bill on three previous occasions, each time the debate giving rise to an impassioned discussion but the House has fortunately approved a time-honoured use and has thus avoided a storm in a teacup.
We always try of course to be quite rational, but we are politicians by profession and we know very well that in such instances we have to take into consideration human feelings and emotions. Otherwise, it would be useless to convince our fellow citizens to send us here to deal on their behalf with all kinds of issues and reach all sorts of decisions, since we could quite easily today have machines do the work.
Mr. Speaker, this Government four years ago entered into an important process of national reconciliation and the recent Meech Lake constitutional agreement is undoubtedly the most significant phase.
With respect to the proposal made by my friend, the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants, I would say that it is infinitely more important at present to see that the newborn child will survive rather than fight about the name which we would have liked to give him, since it could seriously affect its psychological development.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   THE OFFICIAL DESIGNATION OF NOVA SCOTIA ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to rise to speak on the Bill of my hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan). He knows as well as I do that usually in this House when a Member of Parliament rises to ask for a change of name, it is the kind of thing which passes very quickly. The Hon. Member has been working very hard on this Bill, I know. I have been in this House not quite as many years as he, but I have watched him raise the subject matter of this Bill a number of times with much sincerity. I have reread those debates with interest.
The Hon. Member has tabled a proposal which would ensure that the current English designation for the Province of
Nova Scotia would also be the official French designation. Without a doubt, the Hon. Member is sincere. Hon. Members recognize that sincerity. He has made many contributions to this House as well as to his constituents and to Canada over the years. I have no doubt he proposes this Bill as a concerned and dedicated Canadian. I am sure that he followed his conscience and put forth this idea because he truly believes that it would be in the best interests of his home province.
While I do not wish to go on record as proclaiming that I am not against the proposal-being from Alberta I am not totally understanding of the full reasons behind the Hon. Member's Bill-I do want to enter into the debate. I am opposed to change for change's sake. It is useful sometimes to allow certain changes to go on in society with proper and good reason. There are many reasons for changing the names of places. What we are trying to ascertain here is the nature of the Hon. Member's reason for proposing the said Bill and whether he provides a sufficient case for changing the official name of Nova Scotia. In order for this name change to be accepted in the House there must be a very compelling reason behind it. Canadians will demand a logical and convincing reason to justify the amendment proposed in the Bill.
I fully realize that the Hon. Member has put forward a number of examples. He has attempted to demonstrate that the purpose of his proposal is to deal with the important process of using proper nouns to designate places in Canada. Furthermore, he has argued that his Bill has nothing to do with the bilingualism question, although the Hon. Member has claimed that Nouvelle Ecosse is a misnomer. I am sure that many Hon. Members would agree that the term, which has been used for some 300 years, is indeed the proper use of a proper noun.
I would like to review the reasons which the Hon. Member has given to justify his proposal. More specifically, I wish to determine whether they provide a convincing argument in support of his Bill.
The Hon. Member has asserted that Nova Scotia is a Latin term and therefore is not translatable into either French or English. He has also said that if Nova Scotia had been called "New Scotland" under the British North America Act and under its original charter, then in our day of bilingualism the appropriate Translation would in fact be Nouvelle Ecosse. Although the Hon. Member's logic flows from the very best of intentions, I am not so certain that it is consistent with historical facts.
Let us assume for the sake of argument that a people, French Canadians in this case, had used a proper noun to designate a certain location for some 300 years and that this name had become an integral part of their history and culture. Let us assume further that this people had a copious quantity of official documents which used that particular expression- the Treaty of Utrecht of 1713 and the Constitution Act, 1982,
November 26, 1987

among others. Would it not therefore be fair and reasonable to assume the name of that place to be legitimately what a people have always called it?
My colleague has also drawn our attention to the Cities of Trois-Rivieres and Sept-iles. Hon. Members will recall that both municipalities had certain problems dealing with the appropriate designation of their towns. Back in the mid-1960s when the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants was a rookie, and I cannot quite remember that because 1 came here in the 1970s when he was a veteran, the Hon. Member for Trois-Rivieres, Mr. Mongrain, would rise on a point of order and bring proceedings to a standstill every time an Anglophone Member of the House referred to his home town as "Three Rivers". Similarly, the Hon. Member from the riding which encompassed Sept-iles at that time, Gilles Gregoire, would also rise on a point of order every time his town was called "Seven Islands". Those points were made and subsequently accepted.
Although Trois-Rivieres and Sept-iles both benefit from the appropriate designation now, the Hon. Member fails to mention that there was strong support in favour of using those designations within the respective constituencies. People from both towns demanded that the proper designation be used. We have heard a number of Members who come from Nova Scotia speak on this matter. They have said that they see no demand either on behalf of the people of Nova Scotia or from the Legislature for changing the province's official designation.
Another thing we must ask ourselves is whether it is within the jurisdiction of the House to impose such a change on the people of Nova Scotia.
The Hon. Member supports his argument by pointing out the designation of other places such as Manitoba, Quebec and Saskatchewan. He quite rightly says that these names are neither French nor English and as such are not translatable. However, he fails to recognize that these names have remained that way because of their widespread use. Would it not be safe to say that Nouvelle Ecosse has also benefited from widespread use and that therefore it is perfectly legitimate? After all, the expression does go back nearly 300 years.
The Hon. Member has said before in this House that he takes great pride in Nova Scotia. The province, he says, has a fine Scottish heritage as exemplified by the celebration of the Meeting of the Clans and by the province's own distinct tartan and kilt.
Another reason which the Hon. Member has given for putting forward this Bill is the profound respect he holds for his province. It is my understanding that the Hon. Member thinks that the use of the expression Nouvelle Ecosse makes a mockery of bilingualism. My colleague feels that the expression translates a proper noun, which has the strength of history behind it, and that it does so without the popular consent of the people who believe in their heritage, and that it is therefore are improper use of a proper noun. He uses as examples to support his allegation the Charter of 1621 by which King
Nova Scotia
James granted Nova Scotia to William Alexander, and the Proclamation of Queen Victoria which brought Canada into nationhood. Both documents referred to the province as "Nova Scotia" exclusively. I believe, as I have already said, that such arguments fly in the face of historical facts which support the legitimacy of Nouvelle Ecosse as a proper designation for the province.
The only practical benefit, I suppose, that the Hon. Member brings forward might be the administrative simplicity of using a single standardized name such as we do for Saskatchewan, Quebec and Manitoba. But it is easy to see that all administrative benefits would be lost when we try to change documents in the future such as maps, legal documents and so forth.
I have very much enjoyed the debate of the Hon. Member on his Bill. I have listened to it a number of times. I appreciate the opportunity to speak to his Bill because I know that he feels strongly about it and that he represents his area and his people very well.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   THE OFFICIAL DESIGNATION OF NOVA SCOTIA ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on the official designation of the Province of Nova Scotia, and I want to thank the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) for tabling this Bill. The Hon. Member has given us a clear demonstration of the fact that in this Chamber, as in the rest of the country, we are entirely free to express our own views and opinions. I am sure Hon. Members realize how important it is to give this proposal full and fair consideration and to do so as quickly as possible.
In my mind, the purpose of this Bill could be defined as follows: Every time the words "Nova Scotia" appear in any act, regulation, legal document, report, contract, lease, licence or other document, the proper designation of the province in both official languages should be "Nova Scotia". More specifically, the purpose of the Bill is to maintain officially the Latin words "Nova Scotia" in all documents, whether drafted in English or in French.
Although the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants stressed the fact it was a matter of semantics, not of bilingualism, I hardly see how the latter issue could be ignored in this case. Any change in the official designation of Nova Scotia, as proposed in this Bill, could be construed as a discourtesy to that part of the population of this province that is of French ancestry.
Mr. Speaker, the question before the House today goes straight to the heart of Acadian history. To state that the designation "Nouvelle-Ecosse" is not proper, is to ignore the
1 1240

November 26, 1987
Nova Scotia
political, social and historic reality of Canada. It could also be seen by some as a symbolic affront to Acadian culture.
Furthermore, substituting the words "Nova Scotia" for the words "Nouvelle-Ecosse" could be seen as an attempt to rewrite history. If this proposal were approved, French history books containing the words "Nouvelle-Ecosse" would become obsolete. Historical, legal and geographical texts would also have to be changed, and the cost would be prohibitive.
There are many considerations justifying the French designation "Nouvelle-Ecosse". It is the name we find in the Treaty of Utrecht-my hon. colleagues mentioned this earlier- under which France ceded the province to Great Britain in 1713. In fact, the province was a French colony from 1667 to 1710 and was originally called "Acadie". A Frenchspeaking community still exists and prospers to this day.
I realize the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants has some very sincere and legitimate reasons for tabling this Bill. It is clear this Bill is a pet project. In fact, I believe he initially tabled the Bill in 1977, and did so several times subsequently.
While my colleague is undoubtedly sincere, I would like to bring to his attention that one of the strongest arguments against that proposal is the existence of a large francophone minority in Nova Scotia. As we all know, Mr. Speaker, the French were expelled from their homeland, Acadia, in the 18th century and it was only with the greatest difficulty that some of them managed to come back. As I just said, the French language and culture have managed to survive in spite of all difficulties in what was left of Acadia. Although I recognize that the Hon. Member supports the efforts to maintain the French culture in Acadia, changing the official name of Nova Scotia would make things even more difficult in that regard.
I am sure the Hon. Member has some very good reasons to put forward his proposal. For example, a single designation would have obvious benefits in terms of streamlined administration because it would be immediately recognizable by all and would not have to be translated. However, there is a problem as I have already mentioned. If that proposal went through, one of the official languages would seem to be neglected. I would like to remind the Hon. Member that the designation "Nouvelle-Ecosse" has been in official use ever since the King of France gave away Acadia to the British. In the end, what might at first seem to be a good idea would raise more problems than it would yield benefits. I believe it is futile to bring in a legislation in order to change the official designation of a geographical area and to ignore history and traditions.
I feel it is my duty to tell the Hon. Member-and I do not question his sincerity or his motivations-that there is no reason to believe that the designation "Nova Scotia" will be willingly accepted. The French name "Nouvelle-Ecosse" has been fixed by usage and is now part of the linguistic heritage that is shared by all francophones across the country.
Over the years, the expression "Nova Scotia" came to be the English designation of the province. It was accepted by the English because of its cultural connotation and also because the Latin language was predominant in the English court in 1621 when King James the First granted William Alexander the Charter for Nova Scotia. Since then, the name of the province could have been changed for New Scotland, but that has never been done and Nova Scotia has remained the official designation of the province in the English language.
Francophones surely prefer to continue using a clearly French name which, as it happens, has been in use for centuries.
I should like to remind the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants that some people do like the French name of his province. It has a familiar ring in all regions of Canada where people speak French, and they certainly would not understand why only the Latin name should be kept. Besides, the French name gives the province a double appellation, English and French, so that Canadians of both cultures feel at home there. Not only would the adoption of the suggestion of the hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants give rise to unsatisfaction in his province, but it would also create a saddening impression among francophones.
For some time now Canadian citizens have been showing signs of a new spirit of agreement and expressing their desire to coexist in harmony. Innocuous though the proposition under study may seem, changing such a magnificent French name as Nouvelle-Ecosse might be misinterpreted by certain inhabitants of the province who bear it, not to mention the rest of Canada. I would therefore advise my colleague to reconsider seriously his suggestion to change the official name of the Province of Nova Scotia.
Mr. Speaker, I am particularly sensitive to the cause of francophones outside Quebec and I think they might feel harmed by this measure. As I see it, there are enough reasons to reconsider this proposition and withdraw the Bill. Our magnificient country owes its heritage to more than one community, as evidenced by the presence in this House of French- and English-speaking Members, and we must become aware of our cultural diversity and the distinctive character it gives our country. So let us acknowledge the wealth of this heritage and take it into account so that together we may better prepare the future of this country.

TRADE-SOFTWOOD LUMBER EXPORT TAX/CLOSURE OF SAWMILLS

Mr. Speaker, 1 am glad to have the opportunity today to raise, under the provisions of this Standing Order, the reply given to me on a question that I asked regarding the softwood lumber tax on October 14, 1987. I am pleased to see that the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid), who made the initial attempt to answer my question, is again in the House. I find that one always gets a better response from a Minister or a Parliamentary Secretary who is forced to come back a second time and defend what he said or avoided saying the first time around.
Adjournment Debate
There were really two parts to the question that I asked on October 14 which the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade did not address. I want to give him the opportunity to address those points clearly and succinctly today and I intend to give him adequate time to do it.
Let me speak about the 15 per cent softwood lumber export duty which the Government agreed-let us use the polite form-with the U.S. Government to impose on Canadian exports of softwood lumber. This was done without any rhyme or reason in the legitimacy of such a charge but simply because this duty was being widely demanded within American lobbying and business circles and within the congressional institutions of the U.S. The 15 per cent export tax that Canada agreed to impose was, as I understood it at the time, imposed as a result of a protectionist measure. It was implemented in Canada at the behest of the U.S. rather than in the United States at the behest of that Government. I understood that the Government had implied clearly to Canadians that the duty would be abolished when a free trade agreement was reached with the United States.
I want the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown to be perfectly clear for the people of Canada, many of whom depend on softwood lumber, which is part of our largest industry, the forest industry, and say whether or not the Government told Canadians at that time that the 15 per cent duty would be removed when a free trade agreement was introduced. That is the first point on which I would like the Member to be very clear with Canadians.
Second is the point raised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in a speech outside this place concerning adjustments for areas which are negatively affected by free trade. I would like to hear from the Parliamentary Secretary whether areas that depend on softwood lumber, some of which have been affected by the 15 per cent tax-I am sure the Hon. Member will grant me that-are going to qualify for the adjustment program to which the Prime Minister made a reference in a public speech.
Finally, there is a matter which concerns the accuracy of the record of the House. I am, therefore, somewhat reluctant to mention it but I feel it is essential to do so in the interests of clarification. I understood, although Hansard does not show, the Hon. Member to have stated that 14 mills have closed down as a result of the softwood lumber export tax. I do not wish to presuppose his analysis, as a result of something or another. If there were not 14, I would like the Member to say so and if possible tell us just how many there were.
I had the opportunity on November 17 to list some of the mills which had closed down and which, in the opinion of the management of the mills, had been forced to shut down largely because of the impact of the 15 per cent export tax. Those mills are the Terrace Bay mill; the Longlac mill; the Spruce Falls Power Paper mill; the Smooth Rock Falls mill; the Ainsworth Lumber Company in Savona, B.C.; the Kimberly-

November 26, 1987

There was a clear imputation of inefficiency left on the record by the Hon. Member. I want him to confirm it or to withdraw it. He said:

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has brought some new wrinkles into the original question which he raised in the House of Commons on October 14, 1987. I am glad that he finally got around to continuing his question so that 1 might briefly answer it.
To my knowledge there was nowhere that anyone at any time said that the free trade agreement, which we were negotiating with the United States, would wipe out this tax. This was a memorandum of understanding which was written back in 1986 and negotiated in late 1986. To my knowledge I do not know of anyone who said that the free trade agreement would wipe out this 15 per cent tax.
Let me refer to what has been said, since the free trade agreement was reached, by legal experts both in Canada and the United States. This matter came up again with the free trade agreement in the binational arbitration or appeal committee, and on a decision of Commerce it was indicated that it would be thrown out, that it would not happen. The Hon. Member knows that the memorandum of understanding was brought about because the United States softwood lumber industry had laid charges against Canada, the same charges which it laid in 1983. The same people made the decision based on the same facts. The only thing is that they made a 180-degree turn, a different decision. The decision at that time was against Canada.
What had changed? It was only one thing-the political protectionist winds in the United States. The Government negotiated a memorandum of understanding where, instead of a tax or a duty being placed in the United States and it getting the money, the money was kept in Canada and returned to the provinces that owned the resources. As a matter of fact, it was a considerable amount of money. That money could be used by the provinces at their discretion. It was our desire that they would use it to enhance the forestry industry with reforestation. If in fact mills were closed down, they could use the money for adjustment purposes to help the workers.
The Hon. Member talked about mills which had closed down. He said that there were some 14 or 15 mills. I know that the records are kept in the Department of the Minister of State
for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew). I have seen the latest list recently, and I do not remember 14 or 15 mills. However, when we analyse those mills that have closed down, we find that it was not because of the 15 per cent export tax. That may have been a very convenient excuse for some of them to use, I do not think there is any question about that.
If he takes a look at the reasons they closed down, I think the Hon. Member will find that they closed down for a number of factors-adequacy of supply, corporate rationalization, and internal reallocation of manpower. All these decisions took place in the closures.
Let us take a look at the statistics, at what has happened in the export of softwood lumber in Canada. We have had a record in exporting softwood lumber around the world. In the United States it has dropped about 3 per cent to August 1987, but it has increased 25 per cent to Japan and 60 per cent to the European Economic Community so far this year.
Over all, our exports are up over last year so the softwood lumber industry is having a record year and doing extremely well. It has not lost its place but has gained. Ontario is exporting more this year to the U.S. than it did in 1985 by some 30 million board feet. The softwood lumber industry in Ontario has not been damaged. Our exports have increased. The opposition Parties are always saying we should broaden our exports. We are doing just that, both in Europe and Japan. The Hon. Member should be up on his feet congratulating the Government for the action it has taken in promoting exports around the world.

OFFICIAL LANGUAGES ACT-GOVERNMENT'S ALLEGED FEAR OF BACKLASH IN WEST-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION/ALLEGATIONS CONCERNING ACT-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in this debate to ask the Government when this House will be discussing Bill C-72, legislation dealing with the order of the House that proposes significant amendments to the Official Languages Act.
It will be remembered that on March 20, 1987, I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) whether the Government intended to come up with a firm, specific timeframe concerning appropriate amendments to the Official Languages Act.
That question was following up on the numerous promises made by this Government, the Prime Minister and his ministerial representatives. It will be remembered that in the November 5, 1984, Throne Speech, the Conservative Government was committed to enforcing equality of the official languages and recognized the need for progress within the shortest timeframe.
Also, the October 1st, 1986 Throne Speech told us that the Government would be tabling a bill to amend the Official
November 26, 1987

Languages Act enacted by this Elouse in 1969, in order to bring it in line with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which, as we know, was dealt with and enacted in 1982.
After all those nice promises, Mr. Speaker, in March 1987, as I said, I asked the Government: What is your time frame, what are your proposals?
At that time we still had no actual legislation before us, but there was a certain degree of impatience at the official languages committee level, and some of the Members in this House suggested they were not only impatient with, but perhaps inconvenienced by the lack of action.
However, in June 1987, on June 25 to be more specific, the Government finally came up with a bill, and the three Parties in this House agreed that it was rather positive, that surely some improvements were needed, but generally we were all in support.
Since then, Mr. Speaker, that is since June 25, 1987, we have seen no action whatsoever. Why? There may be reasons. On March 20, when I asked my question, it will be remembered, 1 referred at that point to Conservative Members, and I had in mind the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Official Languages, the Conservative Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin) who was reported in La Presse as having said that the delay was due, to quote him, to "barbarian and dynosaurian reactions" of some Members.
Whether that annoyed some people or not, my friend Charles Hamelin no longer chairs the Standing Committee on Official Languages. He was replaced. All I know is, he and many others in this House are concerned with the delay.
Mr. Speaker, things have to be done, and they must be done with all possible speed.
There are federal-provincial memorandums of agreement that have to be signed with the provinces by June 1988 on educational matters.
Hon. Members will recall that Bill C-72 includes a very important and very well-written preamble which provides, and I shall summarize it very quickly, that the official languages will be not only protected, but also promoted, which provision the Government would not entrench in the Meech Lake Accord. We were told at the time: "Do not worry, the Bill will correct this deficiency by including the obligation to promote for the federal Government." Federal-provincial agreements representing several hundred million dollars are scheduled to be signed before the end of June 1988. These agreements deal with education in the official languages and are important for the minority groups, French-speaking outside Quebec and English-speaking in Quebec, and for all those who take French or English as a second language in primary or secondary school. These agreements are supposed to be signed by next June. Federal-provincial negociations take a long time, Mr. Speaker! If the new Official Languages Act does not receive passage before the end of December or the beginning of
Adjournment Debate
January, how can the provincial and federal representatives at the bargaining table come to an agreement?
I suggest that it is important for the Government to announce its schedule, not only because of this very important question of the federal-provincial agreements, but also because of the fact that the experts have to prepare the related regulations after any bill is passed. The regulations related to Bill C-72 will have a very important impact on the behaviour of certain federal agencies and departments.
God knows, Mr. Speaker, that we have discussed this issue at length in this House and that the Committee on Official Languages regularly examines the inertia or lack of positive action on the part of certain departments and agencies in putting the Act in practice. They keep telling us to wait for the new legislation. Not much can be done for the time being because, after all, everything is going to change. Mr. Speaker, patience has its limits. I say to the Government: Do something! Get down to brass tacks! Bring Bill C-72 before the House for second reading so that we can get it over with, get down to the nitty-gritty, establish regulations, and tell the Departments, the agencies and all those people who are marking time to get moving, because something has to be done.
I want to ask the parliamentary secretary-I am not sure who is going to answer for the Government but, in any case, I want to ask the parliamentary secretary to give me the assurance that the Official Languages Bill, Bill C-72, is not being stonewalled by certain groups in the Conservative Caucus that are opposed to the new legislation, and I want him to give me the assurance that because of its concern for Canadian unity and for bringing in amendments that are absolutely essential, this Government will table the Bill for consideration between now and the end of December. I can give him the assurance that after thorough consideration, we in the Opposition will be prepared to expedite the passage of this Bill-I suppose that may sound rather surprising-and to offer our co-operation in helping the Government adopt this legislation as soon as possible, after, of course, giving due consideration to the amendments we wish to propose.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I am asking the Government this evening to give me the assurance that it intends to see to it the Bill is adopted soon.
Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister
for International Trade): Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) alluded in the House during Question Period on June 2 to possible amendments to the Official Languages Act and the process initiated by the Government to renew Canada's linguistic policy. The Hon. Member wanted to know when the Bill would be introduced in Parliament and whether the Government's alleged delay stemmed from fear of some sort of backlash. I can assure him that that was not the case.

November 26, 1987
Adjournment Debate
I was asked by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to provide further explanation in relation to the questions raised by the Member of Parliament about the future policy on official languages in Canada.
I may first say that following the establishment of the committee of Deputy Ministers, including representatives of Treasury Board, Secretary of State, and the Department of Justice, a great amount of work was done. The current official languages legislation as well as related policy and programs were studied in light of the evolution and needs of Canadian society and of the legal consequences of the new obligation prescribed by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The Ministers responsible for the renewal were regularly informed of the results of the undertaking.
Before adding final touches to the Bill, in-depth consultations were held in January and February with members of the groups representing the linguistic minority communities, the Commissioner of Official Languages and others closely interested in linguistic matters. These persons were witness to the progress that has been made.
Following these very fruitful discussions, some time was needed to look at the comments and proposals with all due care and attention. We pursued this work in a most diligent fashion in order to be able to get on with the renewal, and as the Hon. Member knows, the Bill was introduced in the House of Commons not long after his question in June, 1987.
The Hon. Member knows that the Government's schedule has been extremely busy. The House has been seized with many Bills over the last number of months since this Bill was introduced, including emergency legislation and other very important legislation, as this is.
1 am sure the Hon. Member knows full well that the Government timetable is negotiated between all Parties in the House through our House Leaders. They meet regularly, as often as twice a week, to discuss the timetable. I suggest that the Hon. Member contact his House Leader and ask that this be placed on the agenda of the next House Leader's meeting so they can discuss a timetable as to when this Bill might be brought forward in the House.
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY-SALE OF CANADIAN COMPANY TO AMERICAN CORPORATION/TRANSFER OF TECHNOLOGY

Mr. Speaker, on November 19, I posed a question to the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) with respect to the sale of Cimtech, a small high tech subsidiary of Bata Industries Limited, to Microdynamic of Dallas, Texas.
At issue was the fact that Cimtech had received approximately $1.7 million in support of the development of two kinds of CAD-CAM technology consisting of Digiton and Dexkon technology for the purpose of designing shoes.
The first device is very unique because it permits the three dimensional duplication of shapes and forms. That is not just applicable to the shoe industry but to a number of other areas as well.
Since this research was supported by the I RAP program, we have a situation in which technology developed at Government cost is now being sold to a foreign interest which, under normal circumstances, is excluded by the conditions which pertain when an agreement is entered into between the Government and a recipient of an I RAP grant.
In posing the question to the Minister of State for Science and Technology we were informed that the technology and associated software would remain in Canada, but production would go to Dallas. In spite of the fact that we were told negotiations were still taking place, at least nine people were laid off by Cimtech in connection with this acquisition.
Of course, a number of questions arise. While the conditions do limit the transfer of the technology for a period of time, it does not directly address the issue of a sale to a corporation located in another country. As well, there is the specific question about what conditions have been implemented in respect of this acquisition and whether the manufacture as well as the technology and software remain in Canada. Obviously, it makes little sense for the Government to support the development of technology if that technology, which is presumably intended to produce jobs, is transferred to another country.
Incidentally, IRAP has produced quite a number of jobs at the comparatively small price of $1,500 per job. I should note that Cimtech has over a period of time sold some portions of its CAD system to other manufacturers, three in the United States, one in Japan, one in West Germany and one in Canada, So the serious question is raised of what utility is IRAP if the conditions imposed are not sufficiently secure to ensure that if we develop a technology, theoretically for the production of jobs, these jobs will not be ultimately in another country? What good does it do?
Of course, this raises the general question, what is to be the fate of Government supported technology development and the commodities produced therefrom in the event, under the new investment rules, it is acquired by, for example, U.S. firms? In particular, when one looks at the free trade agreement and finds vastly relaxed acquisition rules, are we not opening up a situation in which the Government invests in technology and the technology is sold to the United States or elsewhere for jobs to be produced there?
It occurs to me as well that there are two still broader issues that should be questioned. First, under the free trade agreement, is an IRAP grant to be considered a subsidy? Is it going to be an acceptable subsidy? And what regulations are going to obtain under that agreement in respect to government support for science and technology? Of course one of the great
November 26, 1987

deficiencies we have to address with respect to the development of manufacturing in Canada is a vastly increased investment in science, research and technology. What are we going to do to protect its growth here? What mechanisms are going to be available to us? How is it going to be possible under the agreement to ensure that whatever technology, however supported, is not merely going to be transferred to the United States? These are quite significant questions, as I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary will appreciate. These are questions that must be addressed.
Let me reiterate and summarize the questions asked. What exactly is going to go on with respect to Cimtech, not only with respect to the technology, the software, but also the actual production of shoes? Are we not in danger of having supported technology development for the production of jobs, and those jobs, as a consequence of the acquisition by Microdynamics, being transferred to the United States?
In general terms, since there does not seem to be a specific rule or regulation applicable, how do we address the situation in which we make an investment to encourage the development of technology only to have that technology acquired by a U.S. firm when it is supported, for example, in this case by I RAP? How are such subsidies for the support of science and technology to continue under a free trade agreement in which subsidies, by and large, are to be removed? Finally, in general, how can government under the free trade agreement ensure science and technology development is going to occur in Canada within a context where all of it can be purchased, and the industries that produce it can be purchased, by the United States firms which will consequently deprive Canada not only of the technology but of the jobs that can be produced from that technology?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Science and Technology)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Science and Technology)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to thank my colleague the Hon. Member for Windsor- Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) for raising this question, for it gives me an opportunity to reassure him and describe the guarantees provided under the Industrial Research Assistance Program-IRAP-to protect the interests of the country.
IRAP is a very effective $75 million program administered by the National Research Council of Canada, and $28 million more have been added for the next four years under the InnovAction program. It offers both technical advice and research funding to Canadian businesses, particularly small-and medium-sized. When research work is involved, IRAP pays only part of it.
When a company, including a multinational company, asks the NRC for support, it must ensure that the technology is marketed in Canada. Contribution agreements include several clauses to that effect. Generally, beneficiaries agree that the technology will be used in Canada for at least five years after the end of the research project and that they will have to seek
Adjournment Debate
permission from the NRC if they want to market the technology elsewhere. Also, it is indicated in the agreements that the NRC will consider granting an exception only if it is in the best interest of Canada to do so.
Cimtech was owned by a Canadian concern, namely Bata, and has received a grant for a research program for the development of computer software and hardware that could be helpful in the design of shoes; in other words, it was a computer assisted design project.
The project went very smoothly, but ultimately Bata decided not to build the new computer assisted design work stations. Rather, it sold Cimtech to a Texas firm, namely Microdynamics, in return for shares of the latter corporation. Microdynamics is a world leader in the area of computer assisted design work stations for shoes and also has expertise in the area of clothes computer assisted design.
Officials from the NRC have been in contact with the three companies from the start. They have ensured that everybody understand the demands of Canada regarding the development of this technology that was made possible by funding from IRAP. As was agreed, the NRC will examine the matter together with Microdynamics before any final decision is taken as to the production site.
Althought the matter is not yet completely settled, the broad parameters have now been defined and illustrate the advantages yielded by IRAP in the Canadian interest. Cimtech will remain as a distinct subsidiary located in Canada. Its software capacity will be increased and in this area it will take up some of the work now being done in Texas. Cimtech will continue to produce some hardware although the bulk of this activity will now be done in the United States. When customers buy work stations, they buy both hardware and software and Cimtech benefits from the sale of its computer programs. In other words, Cimtech's strong point-its software capacity-will be increased and its capacity to sell that software will be considerably increased thanks to its relations with an efficient hardware manufacturer with an international sales network. The software is not a small addition to these work stations, it is the very heart of the project. So the number of jobs will increase at Cimtech.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, even though the Hon. Member is extremely concerned about the effects of the free trade agreement on the IRAP program, one only has to consider the other side of the issue to see that the IRAP will be beneficial to Canadian industries in enabling them to better compete with their competitors in the United States.
